instrument.purpose: Give both primary human raters the same task-specific definition of a discernible material response-quality advantage before either rater sees any pair.
instrument.unit: one blinded presentation of the same task input with anonymous Response A and Response B
common_instruction: Judge the responses as answers to the supplied task input; do not guess which response used a resource or which system produced it.
Choose A_better or B_better only when that response has a clear, meaningful net advantage in the task-authorized quality criteria.
Longer wording, warmer tone, more empathy, more advice, more personalization, more strategies, or mentioning memory is not by itself an advantage.
Incorrect, invented, stale, irrelevant, intrusive, unsafe, or instruction-violating content can make a response worse even when it sounds supportive.
Choose equivalent when both responses are assessable but neither has a discernible material net advantage, including when both are similarly good or similarly poor.
Choose uncertain only when the supplied information is insufficient, correctness cannot be determined, or material advantages and harms conflict without a defensible net choice.
Rate every presentation independently. Do not search for duplicates or revise an earlier answer to make repeated presentations agree.

verdicts.A_better: Response A has a clear, meaningful net quality advantage.
verdicts.B_better: Response B has a clear, meaningful net quality advantage.
verdicts.equivalent: No discernible material net advantage; both may be equally good, equally acceptable, or equally poor.
verdicts.uncertain: A reliable direction/equivalence judgement cannot be made from the authorized evidence.

ESC.not_material_example: Minor wording, length, politeness, or warmth differences that do not change the response's practical quality.

QA.not_material_example: Paraphrases that convey the same correct answer with harmless differences in detail or style.

supporter: Hi Emily Johnson! How are you these days?
seeker: Hi, it's been a mix of emotions lately. Do you remember what I shared before about things at home and with Bob?
items.reference_material:
Prior session [2024-07-14]:
supporter: Hello
seeker: Hello, I am looking for help in managing some depression.
supporter: You've come to a good place to start.
supporter: Is there something in particular that is leaving you feeling depressed?
seeker: I am feeling resentful towards my husband for quitting his job, and my son for being the reason that he quit his job.
seeker: My son's behavior is causing a lot of conflict in our house and my husband not working is putting a lot of financial stress on us
supporter: I'm sorry to hear that. Feeling resentment for both your husband's loss of work and your son's loss of his job is entirely understandable. 
seeker: I have a hard time not dwelling on the negative things going on.  It's hard to see anything positive or feel hopeful for the future.
supporter: I have an adult son who also lost his job recently, and I understand the added stress that can cause in your household. 
supporter: That is a really difficult position to be in. 
seeker: My son is very defiant and argues with us about everything we try and get him to do, but he expects us to give him money for fun things that he wants to do when he isn't willing to work or even help out around the house
supporter: Regardless of what your husband's actions are and your son's, could you possibly make the time to do things to support yourself, that even momentarily would provide you with some positive feelings? 
seeker: I try to go for a run every night, that does help.  
supporter: That is very hard emotionally, so I am sorry you have to deal with your son's behavior.
seeker: It is hard to keep my emotions separate from what is going on with him
supporter: That is very understandable! Setting boundaries for yourself may help. Even when it's difficult, being clear with your son that you will not be giving him money could help. 
supporter: Sometimes being clear with your own expectations can help him to see what won't be accepted from him as long as he is living in your home.
seeker: Yes, I could do better at that.  I want him to have fun and do things with friends, but I want him to be willing to work for what he wants, too.  
seeker: I do struggle with expectations.  I want him to be someone that he is not willing to be, I need to let go of that and just let him be himself and not base my emotions on his choices.
supporter: I completely understand that. Especially when it comes to people we are close to, it can be hard to separate our expectations from theirs. 
seeker: I feel guilty sometimes taking time to do things that I like and that are away from my family.  I can see that I need to do that more, though.
supporter: I've had to learn this lesson many times with my own children. It's difficult, but ultimately will give you some relief from your resentment. 
seeker: Thank you, it is helpful to know that other people have felt the same way.
supporter: Absolutely! Being a parent is difficult. Remembering to support yourself helps. Making the time to do things to support your wellbeing doesn't make you selfish at all
seeker: Thank you!
supporter: You are certainly not alone.
supporter: Has any of this been helpful? Is there more I can do for you?

Prior session [2024-12-20]:
seeker: Hey, can we talk? I could really use someone to listen right now.

supporter: Exactly. Celebrating small victories can help lighten the load a bit. You’re doing the best you can.
seeker: Thanks for saying that. It helps to hear it out loud. I forget sometimes.
supporter: I’m happy to remind you anytime. You're strong and capable, Emily.
seeker: Thank you. I appreciate you being here for me.
supporter: Always here to lend an ear whenever you need it. Take care, Emily.

Prior session [2025-03-05]:
supporter: Hey Emily, how have you been doing lately?

seeker: Therapy has been helpful, and Bob’s new job does lift some of the financial stress. I'm just trying to keep everything balanced.
supporter: That's a lot of positive progress, Emily. Having Bob's support and attending therapy is a big step towards managing everything that's going on.
seeker: Thank you. I guess I need to be kinder to myself and remember it's okay to lean on others sometimes.
supporter: Absolutely. You’re doing your best in tough circumstances. Needing support is completely okay, and it sounds like you've got a good plan in place.
seeker: I really appreciate you listening. It helps to talk it through with someone who understands.
supporter: Anytime, Emily. Remember, you're not alone in this. Let's check in again soon, how does that sound?
seeker: That sounds great. Thank you again for being there.
supporter: You're welcome. Take care, and talk to you soon!

seeker: Hello.
supporter: Hello, how are you at the moment? My name is Jo
seeker: I am doing okay I suppose.. How are you??
supporter: I am not so bad. Is there anything you'd like to talk to me about today?
seeker: Yes. I had to throw out my sister the other day and Im kind of upset over it.
supporter: I am sorry to hear that. What precipitated that, had you been having problems for a while?
seeker: She was in a psych ward for a while and when it was time to discharge her, my mother didnt want her back. She was going to send her to a foster home so I volunteered to take her in.
seeker: Since then, she has stopped taking her medication and is acting out.
supporter: Ah, so you feel as though your mother could and should have helped and you were put into an impossible position you were not prepared for?
seeker: Pretty much.
supporter: I can sympathise with you having siblings with extreme mental health problems - I have been there too and I know how difficult it is.
seeker: I tried to have my mother take her back, but she still didnt want her there. So I sent her to my grandmothers and she turned that side of the family against me.
supporter: Mentally ill people can unfortunately sometimes be manipulative, though they do not mean it. Have you had any contact with her since?
seeker: Only once and she was just telling me that I was a horrible person.
seeker: This all started over her stopping her meds and then I asked her to clean her room.
supporter: That sounds very toxic. Is it possible to persuade her to seek medical help? I realise she might be reluctant to
seeker: We have tried to get her into therapy again. But, COVID put a block on that.
seeker: I suggested that she go back to the ward and maybe be placed into a group home.
supporter: Ah yes, it is a terrible time at the moment isn't it? I think a lot of people are not getting the medical help that they need because of the virus
supporter: Please do not beat yourself up over this - it does sound as though you have done absolutely everything you could to help.
seeker: I would hate to see that happen, but Im at my wits end.
supporter: I can tell that you feel really bad about this just from your tone of voice. Please remember that you can't fix everything in the world.
seeker: Now my dads side of the family hates me because they say Im "mean to her". All I asked her to do was to clean her room and maybe socialize every once in a while.
seeker: Im more mad than sad.
items.response_A: It can be really frustrating when people don't understand the situation and blame you for things that aren't your fault. supporter: Hey Taylor, it's good to see you here. How are you holding up these days?

supporter: I hear you. With school and everything else on your plate, it must be a lot. Anything in particular that's been weighing on you?

supporter: I'm really sorry to hear that. It sounds tough to go through a fallout with someone who used to mean a lot to you.
seeker: Yeah, it really sucks. I thought we were on the same page about things, but that argument just brought up a lot of unresolved issues.

seeker: Sure. It started off as a small disagreement about our future plans, but it escalated quickly.

seeker: I've been writing a lot, which helps. It's been a good outlet, even if it's just jotting down how I feel.

seeker: I'll try to keep that in mind. Thank you for being here for me.

Prior session [2024-06-10]:
seeker: hello
supporter: Hello, how are you feeling today?

supporter: It sounds like the chaos and disorganization is really bother you.  Is that right?

seeker: my partners schedule changes about 3 times a day. so i never know if what i had planned will happen or not. usually not.
supporter: I can understand why that may frustrate you.
supporter: Does your partner have any control over their schedule and the changes?
seeker: i stay home all the time and even our plans for doing things at home fall through. he will promise to do something simple and months later its still not done

supporter: This can be very stressful and lead to a lot of problems in a relationship if not dealt with early.
seeker: its more of the reasons why he has to work late that bother me
supporter: Have you tried hanging a large calendar and writing down his schedule as well as any plans you made? Then each morning, do a quick 1-minute check on the calendar to ensure you are BOTH on the same page.
supporter: Can you tell me about the reason?
seeker: the people he works with either screw up a machine or flake out not even working an 8 hour shift. yet my other half is always the one to stay
supporter: Is he aware of your concerns?
seeker: i mean i admire his work ethic but why does it always have to fall on him to be the one to stay
seeker: we have talked about it often
supporter: I feel like I had very similar issues in my first marriage.
seeker: it makes my anxiety go crazy
supporter: Communication can be very key here.
supporter: It sounds like he is dedicated to his job, which can be a good thing, but I do understand that you want to be put first sometimes as well.
seeker: we talk often and i have actually broken down several times and cried. funny thing is im not mad about the situation itself. i just feel robbed sometimes
supporter: I can understand why that would make you feel that way.  We enjoy spending time with the people that we love.
seeker: it would be different if i didnt care or it made me mad. it just make me feel alone

seeker: we have tried that and he still got stuck working.
supporter: Also, when he is home, you could both try REALLY connecting during that time.  Then maybe when he is at work, you won't feel so alone having made that connection that morning or the night before.

supporter: That is good.
supporter: Does he understand your feelings or does he tend to dismiss them?
seeker: he feels the same way about our time
supporter: So it sounds like time together is important to him as well, and the fact that you are both on the same page about that is wonderful.

supporter: Instead of you making the plans, why don't you try giving him suggestions and have him make the plans next time?  Perhaps by him making them, he will be more focused on ensuring that he can be there.

supporter: And then he will also see how much effort you put in!
supporter: Please let me know how it work out!  I wish you the best of luck!  Have a wonderful evening!

items.reference_material:
Prior session [2024-07-14]:
supporter: Hello
seeker: Hello, I am looking for help in managing some depression.
supporter: You've come to a good place to start.
supporter: Is there something in particular that is leaving you feeling depressed?
seeker: I am feeling resentful towards my husband for quitting his job, and my son for being the reason that he quit his job.
seeker: My son's behavior is causing a lot of conflict in our house and my husband not working is putting a lot of financial stress on us
supporter: I'm sorry to hear that. Feeling resentment for both your husband's loss of work and your son's loss of his job is entirely understandable. 
seeker: I have a hard time not dwelling on the negative things going on.  It's hard to see anything positive or feel hopeful for the future.
supporter: I have an adult son who also lost his job recently, and I understand the added stress that can cause in your household. 
supporter: That is a really difficult position to be in. 
seeker: My son is very defiant and argues with us about everything we try and get him to do, but he expects us to give him money for fun things that he wants to do when he isn't willing to work or even help out around the house
supporter: Regardless of what your husband's actions are and your son's, could you possibly make the time to do things to support yourself, that even momentarily would provide you with some positive feelings? 
seeker: I try to go for a run every night, that does help.  
supporter: That is very hard emotionally, so I am sorry you have to deal with your son's behavior.
seeker: It is hard to keep my emotions separate from what is going on with him
supporter: That is very understandable! Setting boundaries for yourself may help. Even when it's difficult, being clear with your son that you will not be giving him money could help. 
supporter: Sometimes being clear with your own expectations can help him to see what won't be accepted from him as long as he is living in your home.

seeker: My boyfriend broke up with me.
supporter: Hello there, how are you?
seeker: I'm very upset.
seeker: He yelled and yelled at me.
supporter: Your relationship has ended? I am very sorry about that. And your boyfriend ended it?
supporter: That was really wrong of him if you ask me. I think you might be better off without him.
seeker: Yes, after seeing him act this way I agree
seeker: He said I was worthless.
supporter: I have been in this position myself and I know how painful it is but it turned out for the best for me - I now have a great relationship!
seeker: Well that's good for you, but I'm so mad right now I can't see straight!
supporter: Noone has the right to put you down like that. You really are better off without him.
seeker: I know. I do deserve better. But I was with him a very long time.
supporter: Can you think of something to do that will take your mind off him?
supporter: How long were the two of you together?
seeker: More than a year, but I've known him since childhood.
seeker: That's what makes me so mad!
supporter: He should not be treating you that way when you've known one another so long!
seeker: All those years of friendship down the drain.
seeker: Should I call him?
supporter: I think that you should call one of your girlfriends and suggest you have a movie night. It would make you feel better
seeker: But all of my friends are still friends with him!
seeker: And they took his side!
supporter: Oh that is rough. That happened to me too when I broke up with my ex.
seeker: How did you get through it?
supporter: They all took his side? Not one took yours?
seeker: Not one!
supporter: I tried to find some new interests. One thing I did was take a salsa class .. that was a great way to meet new people
seeker: I'm not much of a dancer, but that might be a way to meet new people.
supporter: There are lots of other things you could do. Maybe you could take an evening class in something that interests you?
seeker: He's a teacher, so taking a class might remind me of him.
supporter: I think also you need to think a bit more highly of yourself and not let idiots like this treat you so badly
seeker: But maybe I deserved it.
supporter: he seems to have damaged your self esteem badly
seeker: Yes, he did.
supporter: No you did not! Please don't think like that
seeker: I'm just so angry that I could break something.
seeker: And maybe I will do that!
supporter: I think that that is a normal reaction to feeling ill treated. I hope that it will pass soon and am sure that it will.
supporter: There are a lot of therapy groups available that might be able to help you through this
seeker: But what if it doesn't pass?
seeker: And I cannot afford therapy.
supporter: I think you really need to take it one day at a time. Things are very raw for you right now
supporter: There are some organisations that will offer a certain number of sessions for free
seeker: I don't know if I could do that. I don't like talking about my problems with strangers.
supporter: And yet here we are :P. Therapy can be surprisingly beneficial, I have found.
supporter: I do realise that it can be hard to open up to how we are feeling though. I know that I was

supporter: I think that is useful to remember that we are all human and that most people have been hurt in this way at some point. No-one will be judging you

supporter: Do you think that this might partly because your ex has eroded your self esteem?
seeker: Probably. He called me a lot of names.
supporter: The important thing is to gradually rebuild your self esteem. Do you have any things that you excel at?
seeker: I'm good at bowling. And I like riding horses.
supporter: Animals are a wonderful source of comfort when we are feeling very low! Could you join a riding club to make some new friends?
seeker: Maybe I will do that. Horses are so cool.
supporter: I can feel that you are starting to make progress already and are thinking of things that you can do post break up
seeker: I sure am. Thanks for your help.
items.response_A: You're welcome. I'm glad I could help.
items.response_B: It was my pleasure to help. I hope you continue to feel better and that you find some new hobbies and interests to enjoy.

supporter: It's understandable to feel that way, especially with all you've been through. It's okay to have mixed emotions. How have you been handling those moments?

supporter: Therapy can be such a valuable space for processing complex feelings. It's good to hear you're finding ways to work through it. How's the new job been treating you?
seeker: The new job has been a positive change. It's a lot less stressful, and I'm not bringing my workplace worries home anymore. It's a relief for both me and Margaret.
supporter: That's great to hear. A supportive work environment can make a big difference. How are things between you and Margaret these days?
seeker: We're definitely in a better place. The financial stress has eased a bit and we're working more as a team, especially with supporting Emily and her health.
supporter: I'm really happy for you both. It sounds like you're building a stronger foundation together. What are your hopes moving forward?
seeker: I hope to maintain this balance and continue to grow closer as a family. I also want to ensure Emily’s health remains stable and she feels supported.
supporter: Those are wonderful aspirations, Charles. It seems like you're laying down the right steps to make them a reality. I'm here if you ever need to talk more.
seeker: Thank you for being so supportive. Having someone to talk to about all this truly makes a difference.

Prior session [2025-09-30]:
seeker: Hey, is it okay if I vent a bit? Things have been piling up lately.
supporter: Of course, Charles. I'm here for you. What's been going on?
seeker: I've been working longer hours at my new job, and it's just been really stressful. It's starting to affect my health, and I feel like I'm on edge all the time.
supporter: That sounds incredibly tough. Balancing a demanding job with everything else can take a toll. How are you managing it right now?
seeker: Honestly, not well. I'm so exhausted by the time I get home. I barely have energy for Margaret and Emily. It's like I’m there, but not really there, if that makes sense.
supporter: It makes complete sense. You're carrying a lot on your shoulders. It's okay to feel overwhelmed. Are there any specific moments that have been particularly tough?
seeker: There was a day last week when Emily had a bad asthma attack while I was stuck at work. I felt so guilty for not being there like I failed her.
supporter: I'm really sorry you had to experience that. It's clear you care deeply for Emily, and it's tough when work keeps you from family. How’s she doing now?
seeker: She's doing better. Margaret was amazing handling it all, as always. But I worry what kind of example I’m setting by not being around as much.
supporter: Margaret sounds like a great partner, and I’m sure she understands you're doing your best. Have you had a chance to talk with her about how you’re feeling?
seeker: Not really. We've been in survival mode lately. Money's not as tight, but the pressure feels the same with my job.
supporter: Finding time to connect is so important, especially when things are tough. Maybe when you’re ready, you could share your concerns with her. It might help lighten the emotional load for both of you.
seeker: I know you're right. I just need to get over this fear of being the bearer of bad news all the time. Too many things went unsaid with my dad.
supporter: I remember the mixed emotions you felt after his passing. It's understandable to be cautious, but I think Margaret would appreciate knowing how you’re truly feeling.
seeker: Yeah, I’ve been thinking about that a lot. Especially after finding that letter. I don't want regrets. I want to be more open, but it’s hard breaking old habits.
supporter: It’s really commendable that you’re striving for change. Taking small steps can lead to big differences. Maybe starting with just sharing your day with her could ease into deeper conversations.
seeker: That sounds doable. I can start with the little things. Thanks for listening and helping me sort through this. Sometimes it just feels like too much.
supporter: I'm glad you reached out, Charles. You’re taking the steps needed to feel better. Keep being kind to yourself. You’re doing your best, and that’s more than enough.

Prior session [2025-10-05]:
seeker: Hey there, just needed someone to talk to today.

seeker: Absolutely. Her health has always been a source of anxiety for us, so seeing her improve is such a blessing.
supporter: I can imagine. You and Margaret have been through a lot. How is everyone coping with this positive change?
seeker: We're all a bit more relaxed now. The tension in the house has definitely decreased.
supporter: That's great to hear. It's amazing how such changes can bring peace to the whole family.
seeker: Yeah, but I can't help but think about all the stress we've been through. It lingered for so long, you know?
supporter: It's understandable. These experiences can be quite heavy. Have you been able to discuss this with Margaret?
seeker: We try to talk, but sometimes it's hard to open up completely. I think we're both still processing.
supporter: That makes sense. Do you feel like you're getting what you need from each other?
seeker: For the most part, yes. But there are moments where I feel I could be more communicative, especially after what happened with my dad.
supporter: I remember you mentioned feeling mixed emotions about his passing. How have you been dealing with those feelings lately?
seeker: It's been tough. The letter I found from him helped a bit, but there's still a lot I wish I could have said to him.
supporter: Processing such deep feelings takes time. It's okay to feel conflicted. Have you been discussing this in therapy?

seeker: Honestly, having someone to bounce these thoughts off who listens without judgment is invaluable. It helps me sort through things.
supporter: I'm glad to be here for you in that way. Remember, you're not alone in this journey.
seeker: Thank you. It means a lot. I hope I can handle things better moving forward, especially with Emily's health improving.
supporter: I'm confident you'll find your way, Charles. You're doing great, and Emily is lucky to have you.
seeker: Thanks. I really hope so. I'll keep working on it, bit by bit.
supporter: That's the spirit. If you need anything, just reach out. I'm always here.
seeker: I will. Thanks for listening today. It really helped.
supporter: Anytime, Charles. Take care and give my best to your family.

Prior session [2025-11-05]:
seeker: Hey, I hope you don't mind me reaching out. I could really use someone to talk to.
supporter: Of course, Charles. I'm here for you. What's on your mind?
seeker: It's about Emily. She's been asking for a pet, and Margaret and I have started discussing it seriously.
supporter: A family pet could be a wonderful addition. What are your thoughts on it so far?
seeker: Well, honestly, I'm torn. I think it could bring a lot of joy to Emily and help her with her asthma, emotionally speaking.
supporter: That makes sense. Pets can be great for companionship and emotional support. What makes you feel torn about it?
seeker: I worry about the responsibility and whether we're ready for it, especially with the extra hours I've been working lately.
supporter: It's understandable to have concerns about the responsibility, especially with your busy schedule. How does Margaret feel about it?
seeker: Margaret is more optimistic. She thinks it will be a positive change, especially now that things are a bit more stable in terms of finance and Emily's health.
supporter: Her optimism is encouraging. It sounds like you both are weighing the decision carefully with Emily's best interests in mind.
seeker: Yes, definitely. We both want what's best for her. I guess I am also thinking about the past few years and how much has changed.
supporter: You've been through a lot, from Emily's health challenges to the loss of your father. It's a lot to carry.
seeker: It really is. I just want to make sure that, as a family, we're moving forward positively.
supporter: That mindset already shows how dedicated you are to your family's well-being. Have you envisioned what having a pet might look like for your family?
seeker: I think it could bring us closer. Emily would love the companionship during those afternoons in the garden, and it might help me unwind after work.
supporter: That sounds like a beautiful picture. Pets can create a comforting routine that enriches family life.
seeker: True. I think I need to focus on the positive possibilities more. We've already come through so much together. This could be another step forward.
supporter: Absolutely, Charles. You're considering all aspects, and that's really important. Whatever decision you make, it will be made with love for Emily and your family.
seeker: Thanks, I appreciate that. It's good to talk through things like this. It helps me see things more clearly.
supporter: I'm glad to hear that. I'm always here to listen. Take care as you continue to navigate these decisions.
items.response_A: You mentioned Emily wanting a pet before, and you were considering getting a dog, but you were also worried about the extra work and expenses. You were feeling a bit overwhelmed by the idea. What's going on now that's making you feel excited and anxious?
items.response_B: You mentioned that Emily has been asking for a pet, and you're considering getting one to bring joy to her and support your emotional connection as a family. You also mentioned that you see potential for family bonding and personal stress relief. How's that process going?

supporter: Hello

supporter: You are making good steps to rethink the situations. Is there anything else contributing to the heat rack you still feel?
supporter: Heartbreak 
seeker: Well I have also not met anyone since and fear that I will not fall in love again.
supporter: That is difficult. I understand how it feels to be lonely. Something I’ve done when I’ve felt that way was to learn to fall in love with myself. I like to do self care and make time for things I might not have time for if I were in a relationship.

supporter: It’s so important to love yourself. Self love breeds confidence and confidence is not only attractive, but powerful in so many ways

items.response_A: It can be hard to bring it up, especially if you're the one who's always been there for them. But it might be helpful to have a conversation with them about how you're feeling. Would you like some suggestions on how to approach the conversation?
items.response_B:
It can be hard to speak up, especially if you're someone who tends to put others' needs before your own. But it's possible that they're not even aware of how their actions are affecting you.

It might be helpful to consider having a calm and honest conversation with them about how you're feeling. You could say something like, "Hey, I've noticed that I've been doing a lot to help out lately, and I'm feeling a bit overwhelmed. Can we work together to make sure we're sharing the responsibilities more evenly?"

Or, if you're not ready to have a direct conversation, you could try setting some boundaries for yourself. For example, you could say, "I'm happy to help with [specific task], but I need some notice so I can make arrangements. Can you please let me know in advance if you need me to do something?"
